catalogue_metadata.scope_notes: Extracted from a Continuous Architecture System (CAS) that leverages LLM-based agents for architecture governance, knowledge management, and skill execution. Analysis based on public module symbols, directory structure, and configuration artifacts.
analysis_limits: Code content was not read directly; inference relies on symbol names, file paths, and structural clues.
Some agentic behaviour (e.g., exact prompt engineering, tool call loops) could not be verified from the provided evidence.
GitHub Actions workflows were only partially inspected via filenames; deeper orchestration semantics are inferred.

system_map.overview: The repository implements a Continuous Architecture System (CAS) where LLM agents (via LiteLLM) plan, execute, and document architectural decisions against a persistent knowledge store. A central FlowRunner orchestrates a pipeline of steps, while governance engines, compliance checks, and skill-based subagents provide control, validation, and specialised capabilities.

agents.name: FlowRunner
agents.role: Central orchestrator that executes a pipeline of steps, passing a shared mutable context to each step.

agents.name: LiteLLMClient
agents.role: Provides a unified interface to multiple LLM providers, enabling model selection, fallback, and API portability.

agents.name: MockLLMClient
agents.role: A deterministic replacement for LiteLLMClient used to test pipelines without external LLM calls.

agents.name: AgenticMerger
agents.role: Merges governance blocks and agent-specific configuration into the final input that is passed to LLM agents or stored for agent context.

agents.name: ComplianceEngine
agents.role: Validates agent inputs/outputs against governance rules and returns compliance findings, acting as a guardrail.

agents.name: GovernanceActionEngine
agents.role: Executes governance actions (e.g., state transitions, approvals) and tracks a transition registry to keep architecture decisions in compliance.

agents.name: Verifier
agents.role: A dedicated subagent (or rule-based checker) that validates produced artifacts (e.g., ADRs, patterns) for correctness and completeness.

agents.name: SkillExecutors (cas-*)
agents.role: Modular, prompt-based capabilities (skills) that encapsulate specialised workflows such as adding features, generating drawio diagrams, or refactoring knowledge links.

orchestration.description: A single FlowRunner drives the pipeline execution. Steps are likely sequential and share a mutable context. Governance and compliance components wrap the pipeline to enforce constraints, but the control flow is centralised in the runner.

tools_and_integrations.name: LiteLLM
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Provides a uniform API for multiple LLM providers, enabling model-agnostic agent execution and fallback.

tools_and_integrations.name: MockLLM
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Deterministic responses for unit/integration tests, avoiding live API costs and nondeterministic failures.

tools_and_integrations.name: GitHub Actions
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Continuously ingest repository changes, validate governance, and generate/update architecture artifacts.

tools_and_integrations.name: MkDocs (material, drawio, glightbox)
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Renders the architecture knowledge base as static documentation, including diagrams and interactive elements.

tools_and_integrations.name: OpenTelemetry
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Tracing and metrics for agent execution and governance steps, aiding debugging and evaluation.

tools_and_integrations.name: Skills (prompt-based tools)
tools_and_integrations.purpose: Encapsulate specialised agent workflows as reusable prompts/instructions, enabling composable agent capabilities.

state_and_memory.description: Architecture knowledge base (decisions, patterns, rules, maps, narratives) stored in cas-knowledge/global and per-project folders.
Runtime execution profile and rule context stored in cas-knowledge/runtime (execution-profile.yaml, rule-context.json), used to propagate context during a run.
Templates for ADRs, pattern definitions, and other architecture artifacts, which act as reusable contracts for agent output.

patterns.name: Sequential Pipeline with Shared Mutable Context

tool_protocols.notes: Tool calls are abstracted via LiteLLM client and skill steps.

optimisation_targets.notes: Sequential flow reduces parallel complexity at the cost of throughput.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: A single orchestrator with explicit step order provides predictable governance behaviour.

patterns.summary: A central runner executes a predefined sequence of steps, each receiving and mutating a shared context object.
patterns.intent: To achieve predictable multi-step workflows where state is explicit and flow is deterministic.
patterns.context: Appears in the core runner of the CAS CLI; the FlowRunner symbol suggests a loop over steps.
forces: Need for deterministic control over agent execution
Why shared state is passed – to allow steps to build on each other
Want to keep orchestration simple and auditable
patterns.solution: Implement a FlowRunner that holds a list of steps and a context object. Each step receives the context, processes it, and returns a possibly modified context that is passed to the next step. This pattern is common in workflow engines and is evidenced by the presence of a central runner class.
implementation_signals: Likely a loop over steps that passes a mutable context
CLI entry point (main) triggers the runner

evidence.note: Central orchestration class likely iterating steps.

benefits: Simple to reason about execution order
Shared context allows aggregation of results
Easy to trace via logging or OpenTelemetry
costs: Context can become large and tightly coupled
failure_modes: Step failure may halt the entire pipeline if not handled
Mutating context can cause hidden dependencies

patterns.reuse_notes: This pattern is generic for any multi-step agent pipeline; it can be adapted to include retries, branching, or parallelism later.

patterns.name: LLM Provider Abstraction via LiteLLM Client

optimisation_targets.notes: Abstraction allows model swapping to manage cost and quality.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Unified client reduces vendor lock-in while still allowing agent autonomy in model choice.

patterns.summary: The system uses the litellm library behind a custom client to expose a single LLM interface, enabling provider swaps and fallback.
patterns.intent: To decouple the agent pipeline from any single LLM vendor, improving portability and resilience.
patterns.context: The repo depends on litellm and defines a LiteLLMClient in src/cas_runner/llm.
forces: Need to support multiple LLM providers without rewriting agent logic
Cost and capability variation across providers
Avoid vendor lock-in
patterns.solution: Wrap litellm into a dedicated client class that provides a consistent chat/generate API. Agents and steps depend on this client, and the underlying model/provider can be configured at runtime or via settings.
implementation_signals: Mock client mirrors the same interface for tests

costs: Potential feature gaps if a provider lacks certain capabilities
failure_modes: Provider-specific errors may leak if not handled uniformly
Configuration drift across environments

patterns.reuse_notes: Applicable to any agent system that needs to call LLMs; can be extended with caching, rate-limiting, or cost tracking.

patterns.name: Governance Compliance Engine as Guardrail

optimisation_targets.notes: Enforces rules before outputs are accepted.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Automated compliance checks place constraints on agent autonomy to ensure governance.

patterns.summary: A ComplianceEngine validates agent outputs against governance rules, producing findings that prevent non-compliant artifacts.
patterns.intent: To embed safety and governance constraints directly into the agent execution loop.
patterns.context: The governance package includes a compliance engine and related models; it is likely integrated into the pipeline after LLM calls.
forces: Need to protect the knowledge base from inaccurate or ungoverned changes
Agents may produce outputs that violate architecture rules
Manual review is costly; automation helps
patterns.solution: Implement a ComplianceEngine that accepts an agent output, a set of rules, and governance context, and returns structured findings (e.g., violations, warnings). The pipeline can decide to stop, request revision, or proceed based on findings.
implementation_signals: Likely called by FlowRunner or step wrappers

costs: Potential false positives blocking legitimate outputs
failure_modes: Overly strict rules can stall pipeline
Rules may not cover all LLM hallucinations

patterns.reuse_notes: Can be reused as a post-processing gate for any agent output; consider implementing a rule engine for dynamic rule evolution.

patterns.name: Agentic Configuration Merger

tool_protocols.notes: Merges YAML configuration blocks into agent settings.

optimisation_targets.notes: Automated merging reduces manual configuration effort and errors.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Standardised merge of governance config ensures consistency before agents run.

patterns.summary: A dedicated merger combines governance blocks and agent-specific settings into a unified configuration that is injected into the agent context.
patterns.intent: To ensure all agent runs have up-to-date governance rules and consistent configuration without manual duplication.
patterns.context: Bootstrap functions (merge_cas_governance_block, merge_claude_settings) and a dedicated AgenticMerger class in governance.
forces: Configuration can live in multiple files (governance YAML, Claude settings)
Agents need consistent context across runs
Reduce risk of missing enforcement
patterns.solution: Implement a merge step that reads governance YAML and agent settings, resolves conflicts, and produces a single merged block. This block is then stored or embedded into the agent's prompt/context (e.g., via environment variables or files).

benefits: Single source of truth for governance rules
costs: Merge logic must handle schema conflicts
failure_modes: Mis-merge can silently drop important rules
If merger fails, agents may run without governance

patterns.reuse_notes: Useful for any system that needs to inject policy/configuration into multiple agents; consider using pydantic models for validation.

patterns.name: Prompt-based Skill Encapsulation

tool_protocols.notes: Skills are invoked as tool steps by the orchestrator.

optimisation_targets.notes: Modular skills allow reuse and faster iteration.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Skills provide structure while still allowing the agent to perform within the skill's boundaries.

patterns.summary: Specialised agent workflows are packaged as skills—markdown and code bundles that can be invoked by the orchestrator to perform domain-specific tasks.
patterns.intent: To decompose agentic behaviour into reusable, composable units that can be developed and evaluated independently.
patterns.context: Multiple cas-* skills exist under .agents/skills and .claude/skills, with models in src/cas_runner/skills/models.py.
forces: Need to handle diverse tasks (feature add, diagram generation, knowledge refactor) without one monolithic agent
Want to evaluate skills independently
Skills should be shareable across agent frameworks (Claude, others)
patterns.solution: Define each skill as a folder containing instructions (SKILL.md) and possibly supporting scripts. The FlowRunner or agent runtime can invoke skills as steps, passing context and receiving results. Skills may also include evaluations (SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite) to verify behaviour.
implementation_signals: Workflow `cas-skill-evals.yml` indicates skill evaluation in CI

costs: Need to manage skill versioning and dependencies
failure_modes: Poorly designed skills can lead to inconsistent outputs
Insufficient evaluation cases may allow regressions

patterns.reuse_notes: This is a powerful pattern for any agent system that requires specialised workflows; define a stable skill interface and versioning.

patterns.name: Standalone Verifier Agent

tool_protocols.notes: Verifier may be invoked as a subagent after generation.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Separation of generation and verification adds a check without fully relying on human review.

patterns.summary: A separate verifier agent is used to check artifacts produced by other agents, adding a quality gate before acceptance.
patterns.intent: To catch errors or rule violations that the generating agent may miss, improving trust in outputs.
patterns.context: A verifier subagent is defined in both .claude/agents/verifier.md and .agents/subagents/verifier.md.
forces: LLM outputs can be incomplete or biased
Governance requires independent validation
Manual verification is costly; automated LLM verification is partially sufficient
patterns.solution: Define a verifier agent with its own system prompt and criteria. The main flow runs generation, then invokes the verifier to review the output, potentially iterating if issues are found.
implementation_signals: Likely used as a subagent in the FlowRunner or skill steps

evidence.note: Duplicate verifier definition (for different agent frameworks).

benefits: Can be adapted with different criteria
costs: Additional LLM call latency and cost
May still be fooled by similar LLM biases
failure_modes: Verifier may be too lenient or too strict
If verifier is skipped, gate is bypassed

patterns.reuse_notes: Common pattern in multi-agent systems; define clear verification criteria and consider using structured output to make verification objective.

patterns.name: Skill Evaluation Harness

tool_protocols.notes: Evaluation compares skill outputs against assertions.

optimisation_targets.notes: Continuous evaluation of skills in CI.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Automated tests constrain skill behaviour to expected outcomes.

patterns.summary: A structured evaluation system (cases, suites, results) is used to test skills in CI, ensuring agent capabilities remain reliable.
patterns.intent: To validate that skills produce correct outputs and to prevent regressions as the skill prompts evolve.
patterns.context: The repo defines SkillEvalCase, SkillEvalSuite, SkillEvalResult, and SkillEvalReport in src/cas_runner/skills/models.py, alongside a CI workflow for skill evals.
forces: Prompt-based skills can be non-deterministic
Need to measure skill quality objectively
CI integration allows automated regression testing
patterns.solution: Define a data model that captures evaluation cases (input/output expectations) and assertions. A runner (likely in CI) executes each skill against the cases and produces a report with pass/fail status.

costs: Writing good test cases is effortful
Overfit to examples may miss real-world variance
failure_modes: If assertions are too loose, regressions slip through
If too strict, false negatives block progress

patterns.reuse_notes: Applicable to any prompt-based agent capability; consider using LLM-as-judge for qualitative assertions alongside rule-based checks.

patterns.name: Persistent Knowledge Store as Blackboard

optimisation_targets.notes: Store is the source of truth for architecture knowledge.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Agents read/write from a shared store, enabling autonomy within governance constraints.

patterns.summary: The system uses a file-based knowledge base (cas-knowledge) as a shared blackboard where agents persist and retrieve decisions, patterns, rules, and governance state.
patterns.intent: To create a durable, shared memory for agents that can be inspected, version-controlled, and reused across runs.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/global contains subdirectories for decisions, governance, maps, models, narratives, patterns, rules, signals; per-project folders exist. Runtime files store execution state.
forces: Agent outputs need to be persisted and audited
Multiple agents may need to share context
Version control integration is desirable (Git)
patterns.solution: Structure the knowledge base with standardised folders and templates. Agents write new artifacts (e.g., ADRs, pattern updates) into the appropriate domain, and read existing ones to maintain continuity. Governance rules reference this store.
implementation_signals: Directories under cas-knowledge/global: decisions, patterns, rules, etc.

costs: May require schema enforcement to avoid inconsistencies
Concurrency conflicts if multiple agents write simultaneously
failure_modes: Writes may be lost if not atomic
Stale reads can lead to outdated decisions

patterns.reuse_notes: This blackboard pattern is applicable whenever agents need shared, inspectable state; consider using a database for large scale.

patterns.name: Governance State Transition Registry

tool_protocols.notes: Defines allowed state transitions in code.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Explicit transition rules constrain what agents can do.

patterns.summary: A TransitionRegistry enumerates allowed state changes for governance entities (e.g., decision status, pattern maturity), and a GovernanceActionEngine executes them, ensuring only valid transitions occur.
patterns.intent: To enforce a controlled lifecycle for architecture artifacts, preventing arbitrary or invalid changes.
patterns.context: The governance package contains TransitionRegistry, GovernanceActionEngine, and GovernanceActionService.
forces: Architecture artifacts must evolve predictably
Need to prevent accidental or malicious state changes
Support for human approvals may be part of transitions
patterns.solution: Maintain a registry mapping source state to allowed target states. The ActionEngine validates each action against the registry before mutating state, possibly requiring additional conditions (e.g., approval).
implementation_signals: Models in governance/models.py define state entities

benefits: Can trigger side effects (e.g., notifications) on transition
costs: May restrict flexibility for emergent workflows
failure_modes: If registry is incomplete, legitimate transitions may be blocked
Race conditions if state is shared without locking

patterns.reuse_notes: Applies to any system where entities move through a lifecycle; pair with persistence to enforce concurrency control.

patterns.name: Human-in-the-Loop for High-Stakes Actions

tool_protocols.notes: Human review is likely triggered by governance action service.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Critical decisions remain under human control.

patterns.summary: The governance action engine likely routes certain actions (e.g., pattern promotion, decision approval) to human decision-makers before they are applied.
patterns.intent: To combine LLM efficiency with human judgment for irreversible or high-impact architecture decisions.
patterns.context: GovernanceActionService and GovernanceActionEngine are present; templates like promotion_decision.md hint at approval flows.
forces: Some architectural changes are too risky for autonomous agents
Governance bodies need to review and approve
Balance automation with accountability
patterns.solution: Define governance actions that have a 'needs_review' status. When such an action is requested, the system pauses the pipeline and creates a review request (e.g., via a file or notification). Once a human approves, the action proceeds.

evidence.note: Service that may implement review steps.

costs: Requires human involvement which can be a bottleneck
failure_modes: If human review is ignored or slow, pipeline may stall
Ambiguity in review criteria may lead to inconsistent approval

patterns.reuse_notes: Common for financial or regulated domains; implement as an external approval service for scalability.

patterns.name: Mock LLM Client for Deterministic Testing

optimisation_targets.notes: Avoids live API costs in tests.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Deterministic tests are simpler and more reliable.

patterns.summary: A mock LLM client provides scripted responses, enabling offline testing of agent pipelines without external costs.
patterns.intent: To test orchestration logic and rule enforcement in isolation from LLM variability.
patterns.context: MockLLMClient exists in the llm module, likely used in unit tests and CI.
forces: Live LLM calls are slow, expensive, and nondeterministic
Tests need to be repeatable
Mock should mimic the same interface as the real client
patterns.solution: Implement a client that conforms to the LLM client interface and returns pre-defined responses based on input patterns or a configurable fixture file.
implementation_signals: Presence of both real and mock clients in the same module

benefits: Enables CI to run agent tests without keys
costs: Mock may not capture real LLM behaviour
failure_modes: Tests may pass with mocks but fail with real LLM
Fixture drift can cause false confidence

patterns.reuse_notes: Standard practice; ensure mock interface stays in sync with real client and use realistic fixtures.

patterns.name: Workspace Bootstrap and Configuration Injection

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Standardised setup ensures all agents have similar environment.

patterns.summary: A bootstrap step prepares the workspace by merging governance blocks, creating symlinks, and setting up initial context for agents.
patterns.intent: To ensure agents start with the right configuration and governance rules, avoiding inconsistencies.
patterns.context: bootstrap.py contains functions to merge governance block, Claude settings, create symlinks, and init workspace.
forces: Agents need consistent configuration across different host environments
Governance rules may change; must be injected fresh
Support for multiple agent frameworks (Claude, custom)
patterns.solution: On setup, run a bootstrap that reads governance YAML and agent settings, merges them, and writes the combined configuration into the workspace (e.g., CLAUDE.md, symlinks to skill folders). This ensures every agent invocation sees the same context.
implementation_signals: Presence of `.agents` and `.claude` folders for agent definitions

evidence.note: Claude configuration file that is merged.

costs: If merge fails, workspace may be broken
failure_modes: Stale workspace can cause agents to use outdated rules
Symlink errors on different OS

patterns.reuse_notes: Useful for any multi-agent system that needs a shared working directory; consider idempotency and atomic writes.

patterns.name: OpenTelemetry Tracing for Agent Execution

tool_protocols.notes: Tracing spans capture LLM calls and steps.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Observability is added without affecting agent logic.

patterns.summary: The system integrates OpenTelemetry to trace each pipeline step and LLM call, providing runtime visibility into agent behaviour.
patterns.intent: To support debugging, monitoring, and performance analysis of agent workflows.
patterns.context: pyproject.toml lists opentelemetry-api and opentelemetry-sdk; runtime traces directory exists for storing trace data.
forces: Agent runs are complex and non-deterministic
Need to attribute errors to specific steps or LLM calls
Cost and latency need to be analysed
patterns.solution: Instrument the runner and LLM client with OpenTelemetry spans. Each step creates a child span, and the LLM client records model, tokens, and latency. Traces are exported or written to a local directory.

failure_modes: If traces are not correlated, debugging fails
Trace storage can grow large

patterns.reuse_notes: Adopt standard OpenTelemetry conventions; export traces to a central system for production.

patterns.name: Templated Knowledge Artifacts

optimisation_targets.notes: Structures agent output to reduce variation.

simplicity_vs_autonomy.rationale: Templates guide autonomous agents to produce standardised output.

patterns.summary: Predefined markdown templates for ADRs, patterns, rules, etc., are used to shape agent-generated architecture documents, ensuring consistency.
patterns.intent: To reduce variation and improve the quality of agent output by constraining format and content.
patterns.context: cas-knowledge/templates contains templates for architecture intent, ADR, evolution map, pattern, rule, signal, etc.
forces: Free-form LLM output is often unstructured
Knowledge base consumers (humans and tools) need consistent format
Versioning and diffing are easier with standard sections
patterns.solution: Define markdown templates with required sections and placeholders. When agents create or modify artifacts, they are instructed (or system-enforced) to follow the template, either via prompts or validation.
implementation_signals: Likely referenced in skill prompts or governance actions

failure_modes: Agents may ignore templates if not enforced
Templates may be outdated relative to needs

patterns.reuse_notes: Use in conjunction with validation (schema or LLM verifier) to enforce template compliance.

anti_patterns.name: Centralised Orchestrator as Single Point of Failure
symptoms: All steps funnel through a single FlowRunner, limiting concurrent execution.
No evidence of parallel branches or worker pools.

where_observed.note: Central runner is the only orchestration class.

impact: Pipeline latency grows with the number of steps.
A failure in the runner halts all agent activity.
suggested_remediation: Consider a task queue to allow parallel execution of independent steps.
Implement retries and circuit breakers for the runner.

anti_patterns.name: Prompt-First Design without Strong Tool Enforcement
symptoms: Skills are defined primarily as markdown prompts, with evaluation models but no explicit schema for tool calls.
Agent compliance relies heavily on prompt adherence rather than hard schema checks.

where_observed.note: Assertions are part of evaluation, not runtime enforcement.

impact: Agents may bypass constraints by not following the prompt.
Hard to guarantee structured output without schema validation.
suggested_remediation: Use structured output parsers (e.g., pydantic, function calling) to enforce output shapes.
Inject validation steps that rerun or correct outputs that fail schema checks.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Templates and skill definitions serve as prompt contracts, with evaluation harnesses for quality.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Contracts are mostly descriptive; enforcement is through compliance engine and evaluations.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Multiple layers: compliance checks, verifier agent, skill evaluation harness.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Evaluation is both automated (rule-based and test-based) and semi-manual (human approvals).

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: Governance state transitions, compliance guardrail, and human-in-the-loop for high-risk actions.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Safety is embedded in the execution flow, not an afterthought.

cross_cutting_concerns.approach: OpenTelemetry tracing and runtime trace storage.
cross_cutting_concerns.notes: Observability is planned but code-level instrumentation could not be verified.
